title: The Buddha's India and Ashoka's Edicts
bigQuestion: How did Buddhism grow from one teacher in the Ganges valley into a tradition carved in stone across India?

story.title: Regret Carved in Stone
story.kicker: After a terrible war, an emperor orders his words cut into rock for everyone to read.
paragraphs: Around 261 BCE, the Mauryan emperor Ashoka sent his army against Kalinga, a kingdom on India's eastern coast. His soldiers won. But the cost was enormous. Ashoka's own inscription later counted the dead, the wounded and the people carried away in the tens of thousands.

Ashoka did not hide from those numbers. In an edict, an official message cut into stone, he wrote that he felt deep sorrow and regret for the conquest. He said the killing and suffering of ordinary people weighed heavily on him.

From then on, Ashoka's edicts spoke about dhamma. For him, the word meant a way of living: kindness to living things, respect for parents and teachers, honesty, and care for the poor. He ordered these messages carved on rocks and tall stone pillars across his empire.

Ashoka's edicts show that he supported the Buddhist sangha. They also show him urging respect for other religious groups. Historians still read these stones today. They are among the oldest dated writings found in India.
story.think: Why might a ruler choose stone, rather than paper or speech, to share a message?

lessons.title: Cities of the Ganges Valley
lessons.mainIdea: The Buddha taught in a Ganges valley full of new cities, kingdoms and wandering teachers.
reading: Around the 5th century BCE, the plain along the Ganges River in northern India was changing fast. Farmers grew rice in wide fields. Trade roads linked growing cities such as Rajagaha, Savatthi and Vesali. Kingdoms like Magadha and Kosala competed for power.

In this busy world, many people left home to seek answers about life and death. They were called *shramanas* (in Pali, samanas), wandering seekers who lived simply and debated ideas. They questioned the priests who led the older Vedic rituals.
The Pali suttas show the Buddha walking between these cities, meeting kings, merchants and fellow seekers. Scholars use the suttas, along with archaeology, to picture the *Ganges valley* of his time.

words.d: wandering seekers in ancient India who left home to live simply and seek truth (Pali: samanas)
the wide river plain of northern India where the Buddha taught

look.title: A Crossroads Town
look.text: Imagine a market town on a trade road around 450 BCE. Ox carts bring rice and cloth. A king's officer collects taxes. Under a tree at the edge of town, a group of seekers in plain robes argue about what happens after death.
look.prompt: Why might new cities and trade make people more open to new teachers?

check.q: Who were the shramanas?
choices: Wandering seekers who left home to seek truth
Priests who led Vedic fire rituals
check.why: Shramanas were homeless seekers; the Buddha was one of them.

check.q: Which was a kingdom of the Buddha's time?
check.why: Magadha, with its capital Rajagaha, appears often in the suttas.

check.q: What sources do scholars use to picture the Buddha's world?
check.why: Scholars combine the texts with archaeological finds.

lessons.title: The Jains and Other Teachers
lessons.mainIdea: The Buddha was one of several famous teachers of his day, including Mahavira of the Jains.
reading: The Pali suttas name several rival teachers. One of them, called Nigantha Nataputta in Pali, is known to the Jains as *Mahavira*. Jains honor him as the last great teacher of their tradition.

Jains and Buddhists shared some ideas. Both taught *karma*, the belief that actions shape future lives, and both valued not harming living beings. They also disagreed. Jains stressed very strict fasting and self-denial, while the suttas show the Buddha calling for a middle way.
The Jain tradition is still alive today, with millions of followers in India and communities in Illinois. Studying the two together helps scholars understand what was new in each and what was shared.

words.d: the great teacher of the Jain tradition, who lived around the same time as the Buddha
the belief that actions have effects that shape a person's future lives (Pali: kamma)

look.title: Two Paths Side by Side
look.text: A Jain teacher says: to free the soul, burn away old karma through strict fasting and hardship. The Buddha, as the suttas present him, says: I tried harsh fasting, and it did not bring awakening; avoid both comfort and self-torment.
look.prompt: What do the two teachers share? Where do they differ?

check.q: Who is Mahavira?
choices: The great teacher of the Jains
check.why: Jains honor Mahavira as the last great teacher of their tradition.

check.q: What idea did Jains and Buddhists share?
choices: Karma and not harming living beings
check.why: Both taught karma and non-harm, though they explained them differently.

check.q: How do the suttas describe the Buddha's view of harsh fasting?
choices: He required it of all followers
He tried it and turned to a middle way
He said it was the only path
check.why: The suttas describe the Buddha leaving extreme fasting for the middle way.

lessons.title: When Did the Buddha Live?
lessons.mainIdea: Traditions and scholars give different dates for the Buddha, so historians use ranges.
reading: Buddhist tradition and modern scholars do not agree on the Buddha's dates. The Theravada tradition of Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia traditionally dates his death to 544 or 543 BCE. Many Western scholars once used c. 563 to 483 BCE.

More recent research points later. Many scholars now place the Buddha's death around 400 BCE, give or take a few decades. They get there by comparing king lists, the gap to Ashoka and the chronicles of different schools.

All sources agree the Buddha lived about 80 years. That is why a textbook may write 'c. 480 to c. 400 BCE' and add 'dates vary'. Historians call this a *chronology*, a sequence of dates, and they treat each estimate as a *hypothesis* to test.

words.d: the order of events in time, with their dates
a careful guess that can be tested with evidence

look.title: Dates for the Buddha's Death
look.cite: Heinz Bechert, ed., The Dating of the Historical Buddha (1991–92); common reference dates
look.prompt: About how many years apart are the earliest and latest dates?

check.q: Why do books often write 'c.' before the Buddha's dates?
check.why: C. means 'about', because traditions and scholars disagree.

check.q: About how long do sources agree the Buddha lived?
check.why: The texts say he died at 80, and all dating systems use that.

check.q: Which date did the Theravada tradition traditionally use for the Buddha's death?
check.why: Theravada tradition dates the death to 544 or 543 BCE.

lessons.title: The First Council
lessons.mainIdea: Tradition says the Buddha's monks met after his death to recite and agree on his teachings.
reading: The Vinaya's own account says that soon after the Buddha died, 500 senior monks met at Rajagaha. This meeting is called the First *Council*. The monk Mahakassapa led it. The account gives the reason simply: the teaching had to be kept whole.

According to the account, Upali recited the rules of the Vinaya, and Ananda, the Buddha's attendant, recited the teachings, or suttas. The monks then chanted them together so they would be remembered.

Historians cannot check every detail of this story, and some think it grew over time. But it shows how Buddhists understood their scriptures: as teachings carried in shared *memory* by a community, not by one person.

words.d: a meeting of monks to agree on the teachings and rules
what people remember; early Buddhist texts were kept by memorizing and chanting

look.title: The Council at Rajagaha
look.text: The Vinaya's closing books tell how Mahakassapa questioned Upali about the rules and Ananda about the teachings, and how the assembled monks then chanted them together.
look.cite: Vinaya Pitaka, Cullavagga XI; see Rhys Davids and Oldenberg, Vinaya Texts III, Sacred Books of the East 20 (1885)
look.prompt: Why would a group chant be safer than one person's memory?

check.q: Where does tradition place the First Council?
check.why: The Vinaya places the First Council at Rajagaha.

check.q: Who recited the suttas at the First Council, according to tradition?
check.why: Ananda recited the teachings; Upali recited the rules.

check.q: What do historians say about the council story?
choices: It is recorded in Ashoka's edicts word for word
Its details are hard to check and may have grown over time
check.why: Historians treat the story carefully because it cannot be checked in detail.

lessons.title: Later Councils and Early Schools
lessons.mainIdea: Later councils dealt with disagreements, and early Buddhism divided into several schools.
reading: Buddhist sources describe a Second Council at Vesali about a century after the Buddha. Monks there argued over monastic rules, such as whether monks could accept money. One such rule was whether monks might accept gold and silver.
Over the following centuries, the sangha split into several *schools*, groups that kept slightly different rules and texts. Later sources count eighteen early schools, though lists differ.

The Theravada tradition tells of a Third Council at Pataliputra under Ashoka, which it says confirmed its teachings. Other schools do not record this council. Scholars note that such accounts reflect each school's own *perspective*.

words.d: groups within a religion that share certain rules, texts or teachings
a point of view that shapes how someone tells a story

look.title: Councils as Tradition Tells Them
look.cite: Vinaya Cullavagga XI–XII; Theravada chronicles (Dipavamsa, Mahavamsa); figures approximate
look.prompt: Which council does only one tradition record?

check.q: What was argued about at the Second Council?
choices: Monastic rules, such as handling money
Which language to use in China
check.why: Sources say the dispute was over monks' rules.

check.q: Which council is recorded by Theravada but not by other schools?
check.why: The Third Council at Pataliputra appears in Theravada sources.

check.q: What is a school in this lesson?
choices: A group sharing certain rules and texts
check.why: Early Buddhist schools kept different rules and text collections.

lessons.title: Stupas and Relics
lessons.mainIdea: Stupas are domed monuments built over relics, and pilgrims walk around them in respect.
reading: The Mahaparinibbana Sutta (Digha Nikaya 16) says that after the Buddha's cremation, his remains were divided among eight groups. Each built a *stupa*, a dome-shaped mound, over its share.

Buddhists treat these remains, called *relics*, with deep reverence. Pilgrims walk clockwise around a stupa, keeping it on their right, a sign of respect in Indian custom. Many still bring flowers and lamps.

The Great Stupa at Sanchi, in central India, was begun in Ashoka's time in the 3rd century BCE and enlarged later. Its stone gateways, carved in the 1st century BCE, show scenes from the Buddha's life and the Jatakas.

words.d: a dome-shaped Buddhist monument, often built over relics
remains or belongings of a holy person, kept with honor

look.title: Dividing the Relics
look.text: The Book of the Great Decease tells that when rulers and clans quarreled over the Buddha's remains, a brahmin named Dona urged peace and divided them into eight equal parts, and each built a mound over its portion.
look.cite: Mahaparinibbana Sutta (Digha Nikaya 16), ch. 6; tr. T.W. Rhys Davids, Buddhist Suttas, Sacred Books of the East 11 (1881)
look.prompt: What does this story suggest about how much the relics mattered?

check.q: What is a stupa?
choices: A dome-shaped monument often built over relics
check.why: Stupas are mound-shaped monuments honoring relics.

check.q: Which text tells of dividing the Buddha's relics?
check.why: Digha Nikaya 16 describes the Buddha's last days and the relics.

check.q: How do pilgrims move around a stupa?
choices: Clockwise, keeping it on their right
In a straight line away from it
check.why: Walking clockwise is a traditional sign of respect.

lessons.title: Ashoka and the Kalinga War
lessons.mainIdea: Ashoka's edicts express regret for the Kalinga war and turn to a policy he called dhamma.
reading: Ashoka ruled the Mauryan Empire from about 268 to 232 BCE. It covered most of South Asia. About eight years into his rule, he conquered Kalinga, on the east coast. Its capital was Pataliputra, near today's city of Patna.
In Rock Edict 13, Ashoka describes the war's huge toll and his *remorse*, or deep regret. He says he now prefers conquest by dhamma: winning people through good conduct rather than force.

Historians debate how much the edicts show Ashoka's inner life and how much is royal message. Buddhist chronicles later told dramatic stories about his conversion. The edicts themselves are the earliest and most direct *evidence*.

words.d: deep regret for something wrong one has done
facts or objects that support a claim
an official public order or message from a ruler

look.title: Rock Edict 13
look.text: Ashoka says that the conquest of Kalinga brought death and captivity to many thousands, and that this now fills him with sorrow. He declares that the best conquest is conquest by dhamma.
look.cite: Ashoka, Rock Edict 13 (c. 256 BCE); see E. Hultzsch, Inscriptions of Asoka, Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum I (1925)
look.prompt: Why might a ruler publish his regret for all to read?

check.q: About when did Ashoka rule?
check.why: Ashoka ruled the Mauryan Empire in the 3rd century BCE.

check.q: Which edict describes Ashoka's regret over Kalinga?
check.why: Rock Edict 13 tells of the war and his remorse.

check.q: What did Ashoka mean by conquest by dhamma?
choices: Winning people by good conduct instead of force
check.why: The edict prefers moral persuasion to war.

lessons.title: Rocks, Pillars and Lions
lessons.mainIdea: Ashoka's edicts on rocks and pillars spread his message, and his lion capital is India's emblem today.
reading: Ashoka's messages were carved on large rocks and on polished stone *pillars* across his empire. Most were in Prakrit languages written in the Brahmi script. In the northwest, some used Greek and Aramaic.

The edicts urge respect for all religious groups. Rock Edict 12 asks people to honor other sects and not to praise their own while condemning others. Other edicts ban some animal sacrifices and describe wells and shade trees along roads.

The top of one pillar at Sarnath shows four lions standing back to back. This lion *capital* was adopted as the national emblem of India in 1950. The wheel under the lions also appears on India's flag.

words.d: tall stone columns; Ashoka carved edicts on many of them
the carved top of a column
an ancient Indian script used for most of Ashoka's edicts

look.title: Ashoka's Inscriptions (Approximate)
rows: Year the lion capital became India's emblem
look.cite: Standard numbering of Ashoka's edicts; Government of India, 1950
look.prompt: Why would a modern nation choose a symbol from Ashoka?

check.q: What does the Sarnath lion capital show?
choices: Four lions standing back to back
check.why: The Sarnath capital shows four lions over a wheel.

check.q: What did Rock Edict 12 urge?
check.why: Rock Edict 12 asks people to honor other sects.

check.q: In what script were most edicts written?
check.why: Most edicts used Brahmi; some in the northwest used Greek and Aramaic.

lessons.title: Buddhism Fades in India
lessons.mainIdea: Over many centuries Buddhism declined in India, for reasons historians still debate.
reading: For over a thousand years after Ashoka, Buddhism thrived in India. Great monastic universities like *Nalanda* drew students from across Asia, including Chinese pilgrims. Monks there studied logic, medicine and grammar as well as scripture.

Slowly, Buddhism declined in the land of its birth. Historians point to several causes: loss of royal support, the growth of Hindu devotional movements, and the destruction of monasteries such as Nalanda by invading armies around 1200 CE.

Historians disagree on which cause mattered most, and the decline was gradual, not sudden. Meanwhile, Buddhism was flourishing in Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia, Tibet and East Asia, so its texts were preserved there.

words.d: a great Buddhist monastic university in northern India, active for centuries
a slow loss of size, strength or support

look.title: Weighing Causes
look.text: Historian A: 'Buddhism depended on monasteries. When kings stopped paying and armies burned the monasteries, it collapsed.' Historian B: 'Hindu devotional movements drew the laypeople, and Buddhism faded slowly long before the invasions.'
look.prompt: What evidence would help you decide between these two views?

check.q: What was Nalanda?
check.why: Nalanda drew students from across Asia for centuries.

check.q: Which is one cause historians give for Buddhism's decline in India?
check.why: Loss of support from rulers is one of several causes historians name.

check.q: Where were Buddhist texts preserved as Buddhism declined in India?
choices: Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia, Tibet and East Asia
check.why: Buddhism flourished in other parts of Asia, where its texts survived.

lessons.title: The Modern Revival
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1800s and 1900s, Buddhism revived in India through pilgrims, scholars and Dr. B.R. Ambedkar.
reading: In the 1800s, archaeologists found and restored many Buddhist sites in India. In 1891, Anagarika Dharmapala of Sri Lanka founded the Maha Bodhi Society to restore Bodh Gaya, where Buddhists believe the Buddha reached awakening.

The largest revival came from Dr. B.R. *Ambedkar*, the leader who helped write India's constitution. He was born into a community treated as 'untouchable' under the caste system. He saw Buddhism as a path to equality.

In 1956, in Nagpur, Ambedkar became a Buddhist together with hundreds of thousands of followers. Their community, sometimes called Navayana or Ambedkarite Buddhism, is today one of India's largest Buddhist groups. This event is often called a *conversion* movement.

words.d: B.R. Ambedkar (1891–1956), Indian leader and lawmaker who led a mass turn to Buddhism in 1956
choosing to join a new religion

look.title: Steps in the Revival
rows: India adopts the Ashoka lion emblem
look.cite: Standard histories of modern Indian Buddhism
look.prompt: Which event involved the most people? How can you tell from the reading?

check.q: Who founded the Maha Bodhi Society in 1891?
check.why: Dharmapala founded it to restore Bodh Gaya.

check.q: Why did Ambedkar turn to Buddhism?
choices: He saw it as a path to equality
check.why: Ambedkar rejected caste inequality and saw Buddhism as a path to equality.

check.q: Where did Ambedkar's mass conversion take place?
check.why: The conversion ceremony was held in Nagpur in 1956.

choices: Wandering seekers of the Buddha's time
review.why: The Buddha and Mahavira were both shramana teachers.

review.q: Why do books use ranges for the Buddha's dates?
choices: His dates are carved on a pillar
review.why: Theravada tradition and modern scholars give different dates.

review.q: According to tradition, who recited the Vinaya at the First Council?
review.why: Upali recited the rules; Ananda recited the suttas.

choices: Ashoka's regret for the Kalinga war
